clean.rustTarget.title: Rust build output
clean.rustTarget.why: Artifacts Cargo regenerates when it builds. Deleting them only costs the time of the next build.
clean.nodeModules.title: Node dependencies
clean.nodeModules.why: They’re reinstalled from the project’s package.json and lockfile.
clean.venv.title: Python virtual environment
clean.venv.why: It’s recreated from pyproject.toml or requirements.txt.
clean.temp.title: Temporary files
clean.temp.why: Leftovers from Windows and apps. Anything in use won’t let itself be deleted.
clean.windowsUpdate.title: Windows Update downloads
clean.windowsUpdate.why: Already installed updates that Windows can download again if it needs them.
clean.windowsUpdate.how: Settings › System › Storage › Temporary files › Windows Update Cleanup
clean.windowsOld.title: Previous Windows installation
clean.windowsOld.why: A copy of the previous version so you can go back. Windows deletes it after a while.
clean.windowsOld.how: Settings › System › Storage › Temporary files › Previous Windows installation(s)
clean.recycleBin.title: Recycle Bin
clean.recycleBin.why: Files you already deleted that still take up space.
clean.recycleBin.how: Empty the Recycle Bin from the desktop
clean.aiModels.title: Local AI models
clean.aiModels.why: Models downloaded by LM Studio, Ollama or other tools. Delete them from the tool itself so its catalog stays consistent.
clean.virtualDisks.title: Virtual disks
clean.virtualDisks.why: WSL, Docker or Hyper-V disks. They grow but never shrink on their own: clean up inside and compact them.
clean.game.title: Installed game: {name}
clean.game.why: Uninstall it from its store, or move it to another drive, so you don’t break the library.
clean.downloads.title: Downloaded installers and archives
clean.downloads.why: Installers and archives that tend to be forgotten in Downloads.
clean.restorePoints.title: Restore points
clean.restorePoints.why: System Protection snapshots. You can cap their size or delete old ones.
clean.pagefile.title: Paging file
clean.hiberfil.title: Hibernation file
clean.swapfile.title: App swap file
clean.systemFile.why: Windows virtual memory. Its size is set under Performance › Advanced or, for hibernation, with powercfg.
clean.winsxs.title: Component store
clean.winsxs.why: It shares hard links with System32, so it takes less space than it seems. Don’t delete anything by hand.
clean.installer.title: Windows Installer cache
clean.installer.why: Windows needs it to repair and uninstall programs.
clean.packageCaches.title: {name} package cache
clean.packageCaches.why: Packages a development tool downloaded; they’re downloaded again when a project needs them. Use the tool’s own command rather than deleting the folder.
clean.browserCache.title: {name} cache
clean.browserCache.why: Copies of web pages the browser keeps to load them faster; it rebuilds them as you browse.
clean.browserCache.how: In the browser: Settings › Privacy › Clear browsing data › Cached images and files
clean.deliveryOptimization.title: Delivery Optimization files
clean.deliveryOptimization.why: Updates and apps Windows keeps to share with other PCs. It deletes them by itself, or you can empty them now.
clean.crashDumps.title: Crash dumps and error reports
clean.crashDumps.why: Memory dumps and reports saved after something crashed. They’re only useful to diagnose the failure.
clean.shaderCache.title: Shader cache
clean.shaderCache.why: Shaders compiled by games and graphics drivers. They’re rebuilt automatically, though the first launches may stutter briefly. Delete it with games closed; the DirectX one is also under Temporary files.
clean.packageCache.title: Installer package cache
clean.packageCache.why: Installers kept by Visual Studio, .NET and other programs to repair, change and uninstall them. Deleting them by hand breaks those operations.
clean.driverStore.title: Driver store
clean.driverStore.why: A copy of every installed driver, which Windows needs to reinstall devices. Old versions are removed one at a time with pnputil, never by deleting folders.
known.heading: What is this?
known.windows: The Windows system folder. Free up space here with Settings › System › Storage › Temporary files, never by deleting things by hand.
known.system32: Programs and libraries of Windows itself (SysWOW64 holds the 32-bit versions). Don’t touch it.
known.prefetch: Small files Windows uses to start programs faster. It manages them by itself.
known.windowsApps: Microsoft Store apps, protected by Windows. Uninstall them from Settings › Apps.
known.programFiles: Installed programs (x86: the 32-bit ones). To free space, uninstall from Settings › Apps instead of deleting folders.
known.programData: Data that programs share between all users, hidden by default. Don’t delete it by hand: the programs that use it may stop working.
known.recovery: Files of the Windows recovery environment, used to repair or reset the PC.
known.users: The personal folders of each account on this computer.
known.appData: Settings, caches and data of your programs, hidden by default. Local stays on this computer, Roaming follows your account and LocalLow is for sandboxed apps.
known.storePackages: Data of Microsoft Store apps, one folder per app. To clear one, reset or uninstall the app from Settings › Apps.
known.oneDrive: Your OneDrive folder. Files kept only online take no space here: in Explorer, right-click › Free up space keeps them in the cloud only.
known.downloads: Your downloads. Installers and archives tend to pile up here: sort by size and delete what you no longer need.
known.steamapps: Steam library: installed games (common), unfinished downloads (downloading) and shader caches (shadercache).

guide.title: Quick guide
guide.lede: TesseraFS draws your disk as a mosaic: each tile is a file and its area is its size. Folders group their tiles under a header.
guide.find.title: Find and locate
guide.find.1: Hover over the map to see name, path and size. Click to locate the item in Folders; double-click to open its folder.
guide.find.2: When you select a row, its tile is outlined on the map.
guide.find.3: The Composition panel groups space by category. Click one to highlight its tiles.
guide.find.4: Switch the color to Extension or Age to find what hasn’t been touched in years.
guide.filter.title: Filter
guide.filter.ext: Files with those extensions (ext:none: no extension)
guide.filter.size: By size (b, k, m, g, t). alloc: uses space on disk
guide.filter.age: By modification date (d, w, mo, y)
guide.filter.path: Text anywhere in the full path
guide.filter.name: Wildcards or a regular expression on the name
guide.filter.aliases: The filter keys are the same in every language. Spanish aliases also work: tam:, asig:, edad:, ruta:, nombre:, tipo:carpeta.
guide.speed.title: Speed and permissions
guide.speed.1: With administrator rights on NTFS drives, TesseraFS reads the master file table (MFT) directly: the fastest mode.
guide.speed.2: Without administrator rights it walks the folders. It’s slower and skips the ones Windows won’t let you open.
guide.speed.3: Nothing leaves your computer and nothing is deleted without confirming in the details panel.

readme.title: TesseraFS {version} · disk space analyzer for Windows 10/11 x64
readme.desktop.open: Open: double-click tesserafs-desktop.exe. No installation needed.
readme.desktop.smartscreen: If Windows shows “Windows protected your PC”, click More info › Run anyway: the executable isn’t digitally signed yet.
readme.desktop.webview: Requires WebView2, included with Windows 11 and up-to-date Windows 10.
readme.portable.open: Open: double-click TesseraFS.cmd. A Microsoft Edge app window opens; closing it ends TesseraFS.
readme.portable.signed: It only runs signed programs: bun.exe (Bun’s runtime) and Microsoft Edge, which comes with Windows.
readme.portable.vbs: TesseraFS.vbs does the same without the console flash, but Microsoft is phasing out VBScript and many companies block it.
readme.fastMode: Fast mode: the “Fast mode” button restarts the app as administrator to read the NTFS MFT directly (read-only). Without administrator rights it walks the folders.
readme.privacy: Nothing leaves your computer. Full guide: docs/usuario/guia.md in the repository.
readme.portable.privacy: The internal server only listens on 127.0.0.1 and asks for a random key that changes every session. Edge uses its own profile in %LOCALAPPDATA%\TesseraFS.
readme.links: Hard links are counted once; folder shortcuts (junctions and symbolic links) are not followed.
readme.opt.noWindow: server only: prints the address and the key
readme.opt.threads: threads for the folder walk (0 = a single one)
